newsitem.title: USA: No evidence of rise in foul language in US Congress.
newsitem.headline: No evidence of rise in foul language in US Congress.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Despite frequent complaints that politicians are ruder to one another than in the past, a new study on Thursday found no increase in use of foul language in the U.S. House of Representatives.

The study, by the Annenberg Public Policy Centre, was prepared for a bipartisan congressional retreat scheduled to be held this weekend in Hershey, Pa., at which Democratic and Republican legislators will make an effort to forge better personal ties.

Scholars at Annenberg created a "vulgarity index" by taking 11 of the most frequently used swear words from a sociological study, adding dirty words most often used by college students in another study and a few other choice epithets culled from the Congressional Record.

"There was little variation in the amount of vulgarity across congresses," the study found. In fact, the foulest mouthed of the last six congresses was the 102nd, in 1991 and 1992, with 1,076 examples of vulgarity or bad language.
The 104th Congress, in 1995 and 1996, when the Republicans were in charge for the first time in 40 year, came in fifth place with 943 expletives.

President Bill Clinton and many other politicians have called for a return to civility in public discourse. Polls find that voters feel angry and alienated by the sharp tone of modern politics. The study said that perception was partly formed by media like talk radio, where some hosts use foul and disdainful language as a norm, and by the angry tone of campaign television attack advertisements.
Turning to specifics, the word "shit" was used three times by the 104th Congress, four times by the 103rd and six times by the 101st.
However, there was a sharp rise in use of the word "ass" in the past two years, to 33 from 25 examples in the previous session. "Crap" also recorded a rise, from 25 usages to 33.

"The trend was to use 'shit' to describe things and not people," the study commented. "On the other hand, 'scum' was used almost exclusively to describe people ... The most common references for 'scum' were to people in the drug trade, communists and people who burn flags."
The study provided plenty of detail about the word "ass."

"There were references to kicking someone's ass, playing one's ass off, pain in the ass, moving one's ass, sitting on one's ass, hauling ass, stick it up one's ass, one's ass on the line, covering one's ass, jumping one's ass and hard-ass."
Use of the word "bozo" doubled in the 104th Congress -- from one usage to two.
"Bitch" fell from 36 usages to 33 and "fatso" has not been uttered in the legislature since the 100th Congress in 1987-88, when it was spoken twice.
A comparable study of the British House of Commons found members of that often exuberant chamber slightly less likely to use bad language than their American cousins.
